rw: Income elasticity equals the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income, so 20 divided by 10 equals 2; a value above 1 marks a luxury.

ww.0.5, so meals are a necessity: Income elasticity is 20 divided by 10, which equals 2, not 0.5; a value of 0.5 would mean demand rose only 5 percent.
ww.30, so meals are inferior goods: Dividing gives 20 over 10 equals 2, not 30; adding the two percentages is the wrong operation, and inferior goods would show a negative elasticity anyway.
ww.10, so meals are perfectly elastic: The 10 is just the income change, not the ratio; the correct ratio of 20 to 10 is 2, and perfectly elastic describes price responses.

rw: With no close substitutes, a monopolist faces the whole market demand curve and can pick a price above marginal cost, which is the source of its market power.

ww.The inability to set a price on the good: Inability to set price describes a price taker in perfect competition; a monopoly is the sole seller and can choose its own price instead.
ww.Zero profit always, whatever the market: Monopolies can earn positive economic profit, often large, by restricting output and charging a higher price; they do not always earn zero profit.
ww.A legal price cap imposed by the governm: A legal price cap is a government regulation applied to some monopolies, not the definition of pricing power, which is the firm's own ability to set price.

rw: A monopoly sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost, which gives a smaller quantity and a price above the competitive level, creating a deadweight loss.

ww.A lower price and more output: A lower price with more output is the competitive outcome; the monopolist restricts quantity to raise price, so this describes the opposite of monopoly behavior.
ww.No price at all in the market: A monopoly sells its good at a positive price, because it wants revenue; charging nothing would earn no profit and is not typical monopoly behavior.
ww.The same price and output as before: Price and output change when a market becomes a monopoly, because the firm sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and charges more than a competitive firm would.

rw: Price discrimination means charging different customers different prices for the same product based on willingness to pay; business travelers will pay more, so the airline charges them more.

ww.Collusion among rivals: Collusion is rival firms agreeing to fix prices or output; one airline charging different customer groups different prices is not an agreement among competitors.
ww.Dumping of goods: Dumping means selling goods in a foreign market below cost or below the home price; it concerns international trade, not different fares for different traveler types.
ww.A tariff on exports: A tariff is a tax on imported goods collected by a government, not a pricing tactic used by an airline across traveler groups.

rw: The prefix duo means two, so a duopoly is a market dominated by exactly two sellers, who must consider each other's pricing and output choices.

ww.A market with many sellers, one buyer: Many sellers facing one buyer describes a monopsony, which is a buyer-side market power structure, not a duopoly, which counts sellers and has exactly two.
ww.A market with two buyers, one seller: Two buyers facing one seller does not define a duopoly; the term counts sellers, and a lone seller would more closely resemble a monopoly.
ww.A market with one seller, many buyers: One seller with many buyers describes a monopoly, not a duopoly; a duopoly requires exactly two competing sellers sharing the market between them.

rw: A natural monopoly has high fixed costs so one firm serves the market cheapest; regulators cap prices to protect consumers while keeping the efficiency of single-firm service.

ww.To ban the service that natural monopoli: Regulation does not aim to ban the service; utilities like water and power are essential, so regulators oversee them rather than prohibit them.
ww.To raise prices for customers who have n: Regulators want to restrain prices, not raise them; customers lacking an alternative supplier are exactly why oversight exists, to prevent overcharging.
ww.To remove all competition from every mar: A natural monopoly already faces little competition because one firm is cheapest; regulation limits its power in that single market and does not remove competition everywhere.

rw: Money serves as a medium of exchange, letting people trade goods and services without barter, which requires a double coincidence of wants.

ww.A source of insurance: Insurance transfers risk through premiums and claims; money does not insure anyone against losses, so this is not one of money's main functions.
ww.A legal contract: A legal contract is an enforceable agreement between parties, a different thing from money; money can settle contract obligations, but that is not its function.
ww.A form of ownership: Ownership is a property right in an asset; money can purchase ownership, but being a form of ownership is not one of money's core functions.

rw: A dollar today can be invested to earn interest, so it grows to more than a dollar later; this is why present money is valued above future money.

ww.Money loses value only on weekends and p: Money does not lose value only on weekends or holidays; its value changes through inflation and interest over time, not by day of the week.
ww.Interest rates never change in any count: Interest rates change regularly with central bank policy and market conditions; the idea that they never change is false and is not the time value concept.
ww.A dollar is worth the same at any time,: Prices do change over time, so a dollar does not keep the same worth; the time value concept says a dollar's worth depends on when you hold it.

rw: Prices rise 3 percent a year while idle cash stays the same amount, so each dollar buys fewer goods and services; purchasing power falls.

ww.No change: Cash under a mattress earns no interest while prices rise 3 percent a year, so the same cash buys fewer goods; its purchasing power does change.
ww.It doubles: Doubling would require far higher inflation or large returns; with 3 percent inflation and no interest, cash buys slightly less each year, never twice as much.
ww.It rises: Purchasing power rises only when prices fall or income grows; with 3 percent inflation and zero interest on mattress cash, purchasing power falls rather than rises.

rw: Compounding gives 2,000 times 1.04 squared, which is 2,000 times 1.0816, or $2,163.20; year two earns interest on year one's interest as well.

ww.$2,080.00: $2,080.00 is only one year of interest, 2,000 times 1.04; the second year's growth is missing, so the balance after 2 years is higher.
ww.$4,163.20: $4,163.20 wrongly adds the full $2,000 principal a second time; interest should only add 163.20 to the original deposit of $2,000.
ww.$2,160.00: $2,160 uses simple interest, 2,000 plus 2 times 80; compounding adds interest on the first year's $80, giving $2,163.20 instead, a $3.20 difference.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative; by not saving the $100, you give up the interest or growth it could have earned.

ww.Nothing, because spending is free: Spending is never free in economic terms, because the money could have been saved or used elsewhere; opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up.
ww.The $100 itself plus its sales tax: The $100 itself is the price paid, not the opportunity cost; sales tax is part of the price, while the forgone alternative use of money is the cost.
ww.The interest on a credit card loan: Credit card interest is a cost of borrowing, which is unrelated to spending your own cash; the forgone gain from saving that same money is the relevant cost.

rw: A bank account holds purchasing power safely until needed later, and often earns interest; keeping value across time is exactly what a store of value does.

ww.A paper receipt from a shop: A paper receipt only proves a past purchase and has no lasting purchasing power; it cannot be exchanged for goods, so it does not store value.
ww.A coffee bought in the morning: A coffee is consumed within minutes, so its value disappears rapidly; it is a consumption item, not something that keeps purchasing power for use later.
ww.A gift card used the same day: A gift card used the same day acts as a payment tool right away rather than holding value over time, so it does not serve as a store of value.

rw: Real income is nominal income divided by a price index, so it shows how many goods the money buys; this adjusts for inflation and measures purchasing power.

ww.Hours worked: Hours worked measure labor effort and are not an adjustment applied to nominal income; real income adjusts for price changes, not time spent working.
ww.Taxes only: Taxes reduce after-tax income, but real income is specifically about purchasing power; adjusting nominal income for taxes only gives disposable income, not real income.
ww.Tax rates: Tax rates are a policy variable, not a price level; real income removes the effect of rising prices, and tax rates do not appear in that calculation.

rw: Short-term goals are typically achieved within a year, such as building a small emergency fund or buying a gadget, so less than a year fits the definition.

ww.More than 30 years: More than 30 years is a very long horizon, typical of retirement planning or paying off a mortgage, which are long-term goals, not short-term ones.
ww.It has no time frame: Financial goals are defined by time frames, and a short-term goal has a deadline within about a year; a goal with no time frame is not SMART.
ww.Exactly 10 years: Exactly 10 years sits in the long-term range, because short-term goals finish within about a year; a ten-year goal like a down payment is long-term.

rw: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound; these five qualities make a goal clear, trackable, realistic, meaningful and tied to a deadline.

ww.Saved, Managed, Audited, Reported and Ta: Saved, Managed, Audited, Reported and Taxed is an invented phrase; SMART is a goal-setting framework, not an accounting process with audits and tax reports.
ww.Secure, Mutual, Approved, Real and Teste: Secure, Mutual, Approved, Real and Tested is made up and does not describe goals; SMART refers to Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound qualities.
ww.Simple, Modest, Average, Regular and Tim: Simple, Modest, Average, Regular and Timely is not the framework; SMART's letters stand for qualities that make goals actionable, not for average or modest ones.

rw: Net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe, so assets minus liabilities; a positive result means owning more than owing.

ww.Assets plus liabilities: Adding assets and liabilities double counts what you own and what you owe; liabilities reduce net worth, so they must be subtracted from assets rather than added.
ww.Savings divided by income: Savings divided by income gives a savings rate, a ratio showing how much of income is saved; it is not a measure of net worth in dollars.
ww.Income minus expenses: Income minus expenses gives cash flow or surplus for a period; net worth is a snapshot of total wealth, using what you own less what you owe.

rw: Twelve months at $150 adds $1,800, and with the $600 already saved the total is $2,400, matching the car's price exactly, so she reaches the goal.

ww.She will be $600 short again: She has 600 plus 12 times 150, which is 600 plus 1,800 equals 2,400; she is not short, so a $600 shortfall is wrong.
ww.She will have $600 left over: Her total is 600 plus 1,800, which equals exactly 2,400, the cost of the car; nothing is left over, so a $600 surplus is wrong.
ww.She will be $300 short again: A $300 shortfall would need only $1,500 of new savings; she saves 12 times 150, which is $1,800, plus $600 gives $2,400 and no shortfall.

rw: A streaming subscription is a want that can be cancelled without harming health or housing, so it is discretionary spending a person may cut when budgets are tight.

ww.Groceries each month: Groceries are a basic need for food each month, so they count as essential spending; discretionary expenses are optional items you could cut without hardship.
ww.An insurance premium payment: Insurance premiums protect against major financial loss and are often required by law or lenders, such as car coverage, so they are not freely optional.
ww.Rent payment each month: Rent pays for housing, an essential and usually fixed cost that is not optional; discretionary spending refers to items a person can skip, unlike rent.

rw: A small emergency fund covers surprise costs like repairs or job loss, preventing debt; it is usually the first step before investing or larger goals.

ww.Buy a luxury item or two: Buying luxury items first spends money before any safety net exists; a sound financial plan starts with security rather than extra purchases for pleasure.
ww.Pay for vacations on credit: Paying for vacations on credit creates debt and interest charges before basics are secure; a financial plan should avoid borrowing for optional spending, especially early on.
ww.Invest everything in one stock: Putting everything in one stock concentrates risk heavily; a plan begins with safety first and diversification later, so betting it all on one company is unwise.

rw: Budget variance is the actual amount minus the planned amount for a category; a gap shows where spending or income differed from the plan.

ww.The total of all of a person's outstandi: The total of all debts owed is a person's total liabilities, not a budget variance; variance compares planned figures with what was actually spent or earned.
ww.The amount of interest earned on a savin: Interest earned on savings is investment income and has nothing to do with comparing a plan with actual results, which is what variance measures.
ww.The total cost of a loan including the i: The total cost of a loan with interest is the repayment amount, a borrowing concept; variance is about planned versus actual budget figures.

rw: A credit union is owned by its members and runs as a not-for-profit cooperative, often giving better rates and lower fees than banks that pay shareholders.

ww.A for-profit stock brokerage firm for in: A stock brokerage is a for-profit firm that trades securities for investors; credit unions are member-owned cooperatives that take deposits and make loans.
ww.A company that sells insurance and annui: Insurance companies sell insurance and annuities; a credit union is a deposit and lending institution owned by its members, so insurance is not its core service.
ww.A government agency that sets interest r: Government agencies, such as the Federal Reserve, set policy rates; credit unions are private member cooperatives that lend at their own rates and are not government agencies.

rw: The FDIC insures deposits at member banks, currently up to $250,000 per depositor per bank, so if a bank fails, depositors get their money back.

ww.Credit card debt owed: Credit card debt is a liability owed by the cardholder; FDIC insurance protects depositors' money in banks and does not cover amounts owed on cards.
ww.Cryptocurrency holdings: Cryptocurrency is not a bank deposit, so FDIC insurance does not cover it; the insurance applies only to deposit accounts at insured banks.
ww.Stock market holdings: Stocks and mutual funds can lose value and are not covered by FDIC insurance; the agency protects bank deposits, not investment market losses of any kind.

rw: Checking accounts support everyday transactions such as paying bills, using a debit card and writing checks, with easy and frequent access to your money.

ww.Borrowing money long term: Borrowing long term is the purpose of loans like mortgages, not a checking account, which holds your own deposited money for spending and bill paying.
ww.Long-term investing: Long-term investing happens in brokerage and retirement accounts; checking accounts pay little or no interest and are built for access to cash, not growth.
ww.Earning high interest: Checking accounts usually pay very low or no interest; high earnings are found in savings accounts, certificates of deposit and investments, not everyday accounts.

rw: An overdraft happens when a payment or withdrawal is bigger than the money in the account, so the bank covers it and charges a fee.

ww.When the account earns interest at the e: Interest earned is a benefit paid to the customer, not a fee; overdraft fees arise when spending exceeds funds, not when interest is credited to the account.
ww.When the account is first opened at the: Opening an account does not trigger an overdraft; there is no negative balance at that point, and fees at opening are not overdraft charges.
ww.When a deposit is made into the account: A deposit adds money to the account and raises the balance, so it cannot cause an overdraft; overdrafts come from taking out more than is available.

rw: ATM stands for automated teller machine, a self-service terminal that lets customers withdraw cash, deposit funds and check balances without a human bank teller.

ww.Account transfer method: ATM does not stand for account transfer method; the letters stand for automated teller machine, a device that lets customers deposit or withdraw cash on their own.
ww.Automatic tax manager: Automatic tax manager is not what ATM means; these machines handle cash and account transactions, and they have nothing to do with managing taxes for customers.
ww.Authorized trading market: Authorized trading market is a made-up phrase; an ATM is a cash machine and has no connection to stock trading or financial exchanges.

rw: A brokerage firm is licensed to buy and sell securities for clients, so individual investors use one to trade stocks, bonds and funds.

ww.A credit union: A credit union takes deposits and makes loans for its members; it is not primarily a seller of stocks and bonds to individual investors.
ww.A payday lender: A payday lender makes short, costly loans due on the next payday; it does not sell securities, so it is the wrong provider for investing.
ww.A pawn shop loan: A pawn shop lends money against personal items kept as collateral; it has no license or business of selling stocks and bonds to investors.

rw: Without branches to staff and maintain, online banks have lower costs and can pass savings on as lower fees and higher rates for customers.

ww.They offer customers no way to reach the: Online-only banks are accessed through websites and apps, so customers can reach their accounts online anytime; saying they offer no online access is plainly false.
ww.They are not insured under any program a: Reputable online banks are FDIC insured just like traditional banks, up to the legal limit, so claiming no insurance at all is inaccurate and misleading.
ww.They require customers to visit a branch: Online-only banks have no branches, so they require no branch visits; deposits and transfers are handled digitally, making a monthly visit requirement impossible to apply.

rw: Diversification spreads money across different assets, industries and regions so one loss hurts less; a poor performer is offset by others, lowering overall portfolio risk.

ww.Selling everything when prices fall: Selling everything when prices fall locks in losses and does nothing to spread holdings across assets; diversification means owning many different investments instead of reacting to drops.
ww.Investing only in cash and savings: Holding only cash and savings is a single type of asset and limits growth; diversification means mixing several asset types, not choosing only one low-return kind.
ww.Putting all of the money in one stock: Putting all money in one stock is the opposite of diversification, because one company's failure could wipe out everything; diversifying spreads that exposure across many holdings.

rw: Dollar-cost averaging means investing the same fixed amount on a regular schedule, so you buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high.

ww.Waiting for the lowest price before buyi: Waiting for the lowest price is market timing, which is very hard to do; dollar-cost averaging instead invests on a schedule regardless of price levels.
ww.Borrowing a large sum of money in order: Borrowing a large sum to invest is leveraged investing and adds risk; dollar-cost averaging uses small regular contributions from income, not borrowed money in one lump.
ww.Investing everything at the peak of the: Putting everything in at the peak is a lump-sum purchase at one moment, the opposite of spreading contributions over time, which is what averaging does.

rw: An index fund holds the same securities as a market index like the S&P 500, matching its returns with low fees and broad diversification.

ww.A type of insurance for retirees: Retiree insurance products like annuities or long-term care cover are separate things; an index fund is an investment that holds the securities of a market index.
ww.A bank savings plan for children: A children's bank savings plan is a deposit account; an index fund is an investment holding many securities, so it is not a savings plan from a bank.
ww.A fund holding one stock only: A fund holding one stock would be undiversified and risky; an index fund holds the many securities in an index, often hundreds of different companies.

rw: The risk-return tradeoff says investors need a chance of higher returns to accept more risk, so riskier assets like stocks offer higher potential gains but can lose value.

ww.Low-risk investments always pay the high: Low-risk investments generally pay lower returns, not the highest; the highest returns come from taking on more risk, such as stocks versus savings.
ww.Risk and return are not related to each: Risk and return are closely linked; investors demand extra expected return for bearing extra risk, so saying they are unrelated contradicts the tradeoff principle.
ww.Higher returns always come with lower ri: Higher returns are not guaranteed and come with higher risk, not lower; if returns were high with low risk, everyone would buy them and prices would adjust.

rw: A 401(k) is a retirement savings plan offered through an employer, letting workers contribute from their paychecks, often with an employer match and tax advantages.

ww.A feature that is built into a checking: A 401(k) is not a checking account feature; it is a retirement plan arranged through an employer, with limits on contributions and penalties for early withdrawals.
ww.A type of home loan offered by many bank: Home loans are called mortgages; a 401(k) is a retirement account named after a section of the tax code, not a type of lending.
ww.A government tax form filed by every hou: A tax form is something you file with the government, whereas a 401(k) is an employer retirement plan, though contributions can lower your taxable income.

rw: With a match, the employer contributes money, often a percentage of what the employee puts in, which is effectively free extra pay for retirement.

ww.A loan that the employer makes to the em: An employer match is not a loan; it is a contribution the employer adds to the worker's retirement account, which the employee does not repay.
ww.A fee that the employee pays into the pl: Employees do not pay fees for a match; the employer adds money, and a match is a benefit for the worker, not a charge against them.
ww.A tax that is charged on all retirement: A match is a bonus contribution from the employer, not a tax; contributions to a traditional plan are typically pre-tax, which reduces taxable income instead.

rw: Roth contributions are made with after-tax dollars, so qualified withdrawals, including the earnings, are tax-free once age and holding period rules are met.

ww.They are taxed twice: Qualified Roth IRA withdrawals are not taxed twice; you pay tax on contributions up front, and then qualified growth is not taxed again when taken out.
ww.They are taxed fully: Taxed fully describes withdrawals from traditional accounts where contributions were pre-tax; a Roth is funded with after-tax money, so qualified withdrawals are not taxed.
ww.They are not allowed: Withdrawals are allowed, and contributions can be taken out any time; qualified withdrawals of earnings, after age 59 and a half and five years, are permitted.

rw: A credit report lists a person's credit accounts, balances, and history of on-time or late payments, which lenders use to judge borrowing risk.

ww.A person's medical history and doctors: Medical history is private health information kept by doctors and insurers; a credit report records borrowing and repayment behavior and does not list health or doctors.
ww.A person's savings goals for a year: Savings goals are personal plans and do not appear on a credit report; the report tracks credit use and payment history for lenders to review.
ww.A person's school grades and awards: School grades and awards belong to academic records; credit reports focus on credit accounts and payment behavior, not education details or achievements.

rw: APR combines the interest rate with certain fees, such as origination charges, giving a fuller yearly cost of borrowing than the stated rate alone.

ww.APR applies only to savings accounts at: APR applies to loans and credit cards as well as to some deposits; saying it applies only to savings accounts is wrong and ignores borrowing costs.
ww.APR excludes all interest and all fees c: APR does not exclude interest or fees; it includes interest, so claiming that it excludes all of them contradicts what the figure is designed to show.
ww.APR is the same as the credit score, bot: APR is a percentage cost of borrowing, while a credit score is a three digit measure of creditworthiness; they are different measures, so they are not the same.

rw: Payment history is the biggest score factor, and payments 90 days late are reported as serious delinquencies that can drop a score sharply for years.

ww.Keeping an old account open: Keeping an old account open lengthens credit history, which tends to help a score; it is not an action that hurts a credit score.
ww.Checking your own credit report: Checking your own credit report is a soft inquiry that does not affect the score, so it is safe and encouraged to do regularly.
ww.Paying a balance in full: Paying a balance in full shows responsible use and reduces utilization and interest, which helps a score, so it is not harmful.

rw: Paying only the minimum leaves most of the balance, so interest keeps accruing on it, and repayment can take many years and cost far more overall.

ww.No interest is charged on the balance of: Interest is charged on any carried balance, and minimum payments do not stop that; saying no interest is charged is false for credit cards.
ww.The balance is cleared quickly in full e: Minimum payments are small, a fraction of the balance, so the balance falls slowly rather than clearing quickly in full each month.
ww.Credit limits rise automatically and the: Credit limits do not rise just because you pay the minimum, and slow payments let interest build, so the debt clears later, not sooner.

rw: By federal law, consumers may get free reports from each bureau through AnnualCreditReport.com, the official site; it is the authorized source for free reports.

ww.Their local grocery store: A grocery store is not a credit bureau or an authorized source, so it cannot supply your credit reports; use the official site instead.
ww.Any site asking for a card: A site that asks for a card is likely a trap, a scam or a paid service; the official free reports require no card payment.
ww.Their employer's payroll: Employers do not provide free annual credit reports through payroll; the official free source is AnnualCreditReport.com, run for the three major credit bureaus.

rw: Phishing uses deceptive emails, texts or sites that look legitimate to trick people into sharing passwords, card numbers or other sensitive details, leading to fraud.

ww.A way to find the best deals and lowest: Finding the best deals online is comparison shopping, which is harmless; phishing is a scam where criminals pose as trusted sources to steal personal data.
ww.A method for saving money on fees charge: Saving on bank fees is budgeting or account shopping; phishing is a crime that uses fake messages to trick victims, and it does not save money.
ww.A secure way for customers to log in to: Phishing is the opposite of secure login, because fake sites imitate real ones to capture passwords; a secure login is protected by the bank.

rw: The premium is the regular payment, monthly or yearly, that keeps an insurance policy active, which is what you pay the insurer for coverage.

ww.A refund for unused coverage this year: A refund of unused coverage would be a rebate or return premium, not the premium; a premium is the price paid to buy coverage in the first place.
ww.The amount you pay before coverage start: The amount paid before coverage begins is the deductible; a premium is the ongoing price of the policy, paid regardless of whether you file a claim.
ww.The amount paid out in a claim to you: The amount paid out in a claim is the benefit or claim payment; the premium flows the opposite way, from policyholder to insurer to keep coverage.

rw: Term life covers a fixed number of years, such as 20, and pays beneficiaries only if the insured dies in that term; otherwise it expires.

ww.Payments if a person loses a job through: Payments after job loss come from unemployment insurance; term life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries if the insured person dies during the policy term.
ww.Medical coverage for illness and injury: Medical coverage for illness and injury is health insurance; term life insurance pays only a death benefit and does not reimburse medical bills at all.
ww.Coverage for the whole of life, with a c: Coverage for life with a growing cash value describes whole life insurance; term insurance is temporary, has no cash value, and costs less per year.

rw: After the deductible is met, coinsurance splits the covered costs, for example 80 percent paid by the plan and 20 percent by the policyholder.

ww.The total amount that the insurer will e: The most an insurer will pay is a coverage limit or out-of-pocket maximum structure; coinsurance is instead the percentage split of costs once the deductible is met.
ww.A refund of premiums that went unused by: Refunds of unused premiums are not part of health plans; coinsurance is a cost sharing term for the percent of each covered bill you pay.
ww.The monthly premium that the policyholde: The monthly premium is the fixed fee for keeping the plan; coinsurance is a share of the actual costs of care after you use services.

rw: The patient pays the $500 deductible, then 20 percent of the remaining $5,000, which is $1,000, for a total of $1,500.

ww.$1,000: A $1,000 total counts only the 20 percent of $5,000 and forgets the $500 deductible the patient pays first; the right total is $1,500.
ww.$1,100: $1,100 wrongly takes 20 percent of the full $5,500 bill; coinsurance applies only after subtracting the deductible, which leaves $5,000, so the total is $1,500.
ww.$500: The deductible alone is $500; the patient also owes 20 percent coinsurance on the remaining $5,000, which adds $1,000, for a total of $1,500.

rw: An umbrella policy adds extra liability coverage once the limits on auto or home policies are used up, protecting savings and assets from big lawsuits.

ww.Coverage that applies only for rainy day: Umbrella policies address liability claims and lawsuits, not weather; they do not cover only storms, and rainy days are not what the name means.
ww.A refund of the premiums paid by the pol: Premiums paid are never refunded under an umbrella policy; it is liability protection that applies when claims exceed the limits of other insurance policies.
ww.Free repairs for any item that a person: An umbrella policy does not repair belongings; it pays for legal liability claims and defense when you are sued beyond other policy limits, not for fixing things.

rw: Disability insurance pays a share of your income, often 60 percent, when a covered illness or injury stops you from working, supporting your bills.

ww.The purchase cost of a home for the fami: Disability insurance does not pay for a home purchase; it is designed to replace part of earnings when illness or injury prevents a person from working.
ww.A credit card that was lost or stolen on: A lost or stolen card is handled by card issuers' fraud protections; disability insurance replaces earnings after a health condition keeps you from working.
ww.The cost of a vacation that a person pla: Vacation costs are optional spending, not an insured loss; disability insurance replaces lost income when a covered health problem stops a person from working.

rw: A financial goal is a specific target for money, such as saving for a car or retirement, that gives direction and a way to measure progress.

ww.A list of the bills that arrive in the m: A list of monthly bills is a record of expenses, not a goal; a goal is a target outcome a person is working toward with money.
ww.A fee that banks charge for keeping an a: A monthly fee for keeping an account open is a bank charge, not a goal; goals are personal targets people set for their money.
ww.A tax that must be paid by every adult i: A required tax on every adult is not a goal; financial goals are personal choices, and taxes are obligations set by law rather than targets you choose.

rw: Saving $200 in two months finishes within a year, so it is a short-term goal; its target and deadline are close and easy to reach.

ww.Building a college fund for a child who: A newborn's college fund takes nearly two decades to build, which makes it a long-term goal rather than a short-term one achievable within about a year.
ww.Saving enough to buy a house in ten year: Buying a house in ten years has a ten-year horizon, so it is a long-term goal, even though it involves regularly saving a set amount.
ww.Paying off a thirty-year mortgage on a h: Paying off a thirty-year mortgage takes decades, so it is a long-term goal; short-term goals are generally reached within a year or less.

rw: Retirement is saved for over decades, with contributions and growth across a whole career; any goal that takes many years to reach is long-term.

ww.Setting aside money for next month's pho: Setting aside money for next month's phone bill or rent is a near-term need to be met within weeks, so it counts as a short-term goal.
ww.Saving for a movie ticket and snacks for: Saving for a movie ticket this weekend takes only days, which makes it a short-term goal rather than something requiring many years of planning.
ww.Buying lunch with this week's allowance: Buying lunch with this week's allowance is an immediate spending choice made within days, so it is short-term and needs no long planning horizon.

rw: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound; each quality makes a goal clearer, easier to track, realistic, meaningful and set to a deadline.

ww.Secret, Modest, Automatic, Random and Te: The words Secret, Modest, Automatic, Random and Temporary are invented; SMART is a real framework whose letters mean Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
ww.Simple, Memorable, Awesome, Rare and Tou: Simple, Memorable, Awesome, Rare and Tough is not the framework; SMART means a goal should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and have a time limit.
ww.Safe, Mild, Average, Reliable and Typica: Safe, Mild, Average, Reliable and Typical does not match the framework; SMART describes goals that are clear and trackable, not mild or average ones.

rw: This goal names an amount of $1,200, a purpose, a 12 month deadline and a plan of $100 monthly, and 100 times 12 equals 1,200, so it is SMART.

ww.Save a lot of money for something big in: Saving a lot for something big in the future has no amount, no purpose and no deadline, so it fails the specific, measurable and time-bound tests.
ww.Try to spend less money on random things: Trying to spend less is vague, with no target amount, no time limit and no way to tell whether it was achieved, so it is not SMART.
ww.Hope to become wealthy someday soon, wit: Hoping to become wealthy someday has no number, deadline or plan, and wealthy is undefined, so it cannot be measured or achieved on a schedule.

rw: A need is essential for survival and well-being, such as food, housing and health care, while a want is nice to have but not required.

ww.A want is always required by law to buy: Wants are not required by law; a want is something nice to have, while needs such as food and shelter are things you must have to live.
ww.A need costs more money than a want does: Cost does not define a need; some needs are cheap and some wants are expensive, since the difference is whether the item is essential.
ww.A need can only be bought with a credit: Needs can be bought with cash, debit or credit alike; the payment method does not decide whether something is a need or a want.

rw: Basic health insurance protects against high medical bills and gives access to care, which is essential to well-being and financial security, so it is a need.

ww.A premium streaming subscription for all: A premium streaming subscription is entertainment you can live without, which makes it a want rather than a need, and it can be cancelled.
ww.The newest gaming console on the market: The newest gaming console is a luxury entertainment product that nobody requires to live or work, so it is a want, not a need.
ww.A designer handbag from a luxury brand: A designer handbag is a luxury product; a cheaper bag works equally well, so the brand and style make it a want.

rw: A budget is a plan that assigns income to spending, saving and giving, helping you cover needs, reach goals and avoid spending more than you earn.

ww.A tax form filed each spring with the st: A tax form filed with the state reports income and taxes owed; a budget is a personal plan for how to use income, not a government filing.
ww.A record of the money a bank has lent ou: Money lent out to customers is a bank's loan record; a budget is a person's own plan for income and spending, not a bank ledger.
ww.A list of the stocks a person owns and t: A list of stocks and prices paid is an investment portfolio record; a budget plans how income is spent and saved, rather than tracking holdings.

rw: The 50/30/20 guideline puts half of after-tax income toward needs, 30 percent toward wants and 20 percent toward savings and paying down debt, giving a simple spending framework.

ww.50% to taxes, 30% to wants, 20% to gifts: Taxes and gifts and fees are not the categories of this guideline; its three parts are needs, wants, and savings plus debt repayment, in 50, 30 and 20 percent.
ww.50% to savings, 30% to debt repayment an: This reverses the weights; the guideline puts 50 percent in needs, not savings, and 20 percent, not 30, into savings and debt repayment, so this version is wrong.
ww.50% to wants, 30% to needs, 20% to taxes: Putting 50 percent in wants and only 30 percent in needs reverses the guideline; needs get 50 percent, wants 30, and savings with debt repayment get 20 percent.

rw: Twenty percent of $2,000 take-home pay is 0.20 times 2,000, which equals $400; that portion goes to savings and debt repayment under the guideline.

ww.$1,000: $1,000 is 50 percent of $2,000, which is the needs share; the savings and debt repayment portion is 20 percent, which comes to $400.
ww.$200: $200 is only 10 percent of $2,000; the guideline sets aside 20 percent for savings and debt repayment, so 0.20 times 2,000 equals $400.
ww.$600: $600 is 30 percent of $2,000, which is the share for wants; savings and debt repayment get 20 percent, so the figure is $400.

rw: A fixed expense, like rent or a loan payment, stays the same amount every month, which makes it predictable and easy to plan into a budget.

ww.A cost that is paid with a gift card at: Paying with a gift card describes a payment method, not an expense type; a fixed expense is defined by its amount staying the same each month.
ww.A cost that changes with each purchase,: Costs that change with each purchase, such as groceries, are variable expenses; fixed expenses do not change from month to month, so this describes the opposite type.
ww.A cost that only happens by surprise and: A surprise cost that cannot be planned is an unexpected expense; fixed expenses are regular and known ahead of time, so they can be planned.

rw: Variable expenses change from month to month, as with entertainment, dining out or clothing, depending on choices and usage, so they require more careful tracking.

ww.A cost that is always equal to income fo: Variable expenses do not always equal income; they are costs that vary month to month, and income is a separate amount that spending can fall below.
ww.A cost that is exactly the same every mo: A cost that is exactly the same each month, like rent, is a fixed expense; variable expenses change in amount, so this describes the opposite.
ww.A cost that is paid only once in a lifet: A cost paid once in a lifetime is a rare event, not a recurring monthly category; variable expenses occur regularly but their amounts change each month.

rw: An emergency fund is savings set aside for unexpected costs, such as a car repair or job loss, so you avoid borrowing or selling investments.

ww.Money borrowed from a friend to pay for: Borrowing from a friend creates a debt and is not a fund; an emergency fund consists of your own saved money for surprises.
ww.Money invested in a risky stock for fast: A risky stock can lose value quickly, which defeats the purpose; an emergency fund must remain safe and available, not exposed to market swings.
ww.Money set aside for a vacation or a trip: Vacation savings are for a planned, optional event; an emergency fund covers unexpected costs, so a planned trip is a different savings goal.

rw: A savings account keeps money safe, often insured, and available quickly when an emergency happens, while also earning some interest, which suits an emergency fund.

ww.A risky stock that could lose value over: A risky stock can fall in value suddenly just when you need cash, so it is a poor place for an emergency fund meant to be safe.
ww.Cash hidden in a shoebox at home or in a: Cash hidden at home earns no interest and can be lost, stolen or destroyed; a bank account is safer and often insured while staying accessible.
ww.A long-term account that charges a penal: A long-term account with withdrawal penalties makes cash hard to reach in an emergency, since you would lose part of it; liquidity matters here.

rw: Pay yourself first means moving money into savings right when you are paid, before spending on other items, so saving happens automatically and consistently.

ww.Spending on wants before paying any of t: Spending on wants before bills is the opposite of good planning; paying yourself first means setting aside savings before you spend on other things.
ww.Borrowing money to give yourself a bonus: Borrowing money to give yourself a bonus adds debt and does not build savings; paying yourself first means saving part of income first.
ww.Skipping savings until all of your wants: Skipping savings until wants are bought usually leaves nothing to save; paying yourself first reverses this order by saving first and spending what remains afterward.

rw: Net worth equals total assets minus total liabilities, so it shows what you own after subtracting what you owe; a growing figure signals improving finances.

ww.Total spending in a month or year: Total spending in a month or year is cash outflow or expenses; net worth measures wealth at one moment as assets minus liabilities.
ww.Total taxes paid in a year by firms: Taxes paid by firms are a business tax measure, not a personal wealth figure; net worth is what a person owns less what they owe.
ww.Total income earned in a single year: Income earned in a year is a flow of money over time; net worth is a stock measured at a point in time, using assets and debts.

rw: Net worth equals assets minus liabilities, so 25,000 minus 8,000 equals 17,000; Dana owns $17,000 more than she owes.

ww.$33,000: $33,000 adds the debt to the assets, but debts reduce net worth; the correct calculation subtracts 8,000 from 25,000 to get 17,000.
ww.$8,000: $8,000 is only her debt, which is her liabilities; net worth subtracts that from her assets, so 25,000 minus 8,000 gives 17,000.
ww.$25,000: $25,000 is just her assets and ignores the $8,000 she owes; subtracting the liabilities gives a net worth of $17,000, not $25,000.

rw: Discretionary income is what remains after taxes and essential costs like housing and food are paid, so it is free to be saved or spent.

ww.Money needed for rent and food in a mont: Money needed for rent and food is spent on essentials, so it is not discretionary; discretionary income is what remains after those necessary costs are covered.
ww.Money earned before taxes are taken out: Money earned before taxes is gross income; discretionary income is calculated after taxes and essential expenses, which leaves money to spend freely.
ww.Money owed to creditors and lenders: Money owed to creditors is debt, a liability; discretionary income is the money you may use freely, after paying taxes and necessary expenses.

rw: A budget starts from knowing how much money comes in and where it goes now, so you total monthly income and track current spending.

ww.Ignoring small purchases entirely when t: Ignoring small purchases hides real spending, since small items add up over a month; accurate tracking should include every purchase to be complete.
ww.Picking the costliest items to buy first: Buying costly items first reverses planning; a budget starts with income and current spending, and then expenses are fit around what is available.
ww.Taking out a loan to cover expected cost: Taking out a loan to cover yearly costs adds debt before checking what you earn and spend; the first step is understanding income and expenses.

rw: To close the gap Sam should lower flexible costs and raise earnings, since the plan only works if income covers expenses; variable costs are easiest to trim.

ww.Stop tracking spending to reduce stress: Stopping tracking hides the problem without fixing it; Sam's spending still exceeds income, so the shortfall continues and debt builds if nothing changes.
ww.Borrow more each month to cover the gap: Borrowing more each month to cover the gap adds debt and interest, making the shortfall bigger over time rather than solving it.
ww.Spend even more so the budget looks bigg: Spending more makes the shortfall worse; a budget gets balanced by cutting costs or raising income, not by spending higher amounts.

rw: A surplus occurs when income is greater than expenses, leaving extra money that can go to savings, debt repayment or goals.

ww.Savings that have all been spent: Savings that have been spent describes depleted funds, not a surplus; a surplus appears when income exceeds expenses in a period.
ww.Expenses that are greater than income: Expenses greater than income is a deficit, the opposite of a surplus; in that case spending exceeds what comes in during the period.
ww.Income that equals expenses exactly: Income that exactly equals expenses is a balanced budget, with nothing left over; a surplus needs income to be higher than spending.

rw: A deficit occurs when expenses are greater than income, leaving a shortfall that must be covered by savings or borrowing unless spending is reduced.

ww.Income and expenses that match up: Income and expenses that match is a balanced budget; a deficit exists only when spending exceeds the money coming in during the period.
ww.Money kept for retirement in a fund: Money kept in a retirement fund is savings, an asset; a deficit is a shortfall in the budget, not funds set aside for later.
ww.Income greater than expenses after bills: Income greater than expenses is a surplus, the opposite of a deficit; a deficit arises when you spend more than you earn.

rw: Income, prices and goals change over time, so a regular review keeps the budget realistic and useful for current needs.

ww.A budget never needs any change at all: A budget does need changes, because circumstances shift; claiming it never needs any change ignores job changes, price increases and new goals.
ww.Banks require a new budget each week: Banks do not require a weekly budget; reviews are for your own benefit, and monthly or quarterly checks are typical, not a bank rule.
ww.Budgets are illegal after one month pass: Budgets are not illegal after a month; they are personal tools with no legal expiry, and reviewing one regularly is simply good practice.

rw: With inflation, prices rise, so the same amount of money buys less in the future; a long-term goal may need a larger target to cover costs.

ww.It has no effect on savings goals: Inflation does affect long-term goals, because prices rise over years and shrink the purchasing power of saved money, so claiming no effect is incorrect.
ww.It guarantees extra interest: Inflation does not guarantee interest; interest depends on the account or investment, and inflation reduces what the saved money can buy rather than adding to it.
ww.It makes the goal cheaper later: Inflation raises prices over time, so goals become more expensive later, not cheaper; the savings target needs to grow to keep up.

rw: Opportunity cost is what you give up by choosing one use of money, such as the other item or saving option you could have chosen.

ww.The interest paid on a loan to the bank: Interest on a loan is the cost of borrowing; opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up by making a choice.
ww.The tax charged on a purchase at checkou: Sales tax is a charge added at checkout and is part of the price paid; opportunity cost refers to the alternative you forgo, not a tax.
ww.The fee charged for withdrawing from an: An ATM withdrawal fee is a service charge for using a machine; opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up by a choice.

rw: A financial plan organizes money decisions around goals, such as saving, investing, protecting and spending, so that choices support what you want to achieve over time.

ww.To make sure no money is spent in a mont: A plan does not aim for zero spending, which is unrealistic; it guides spending and saving toward goals, and people still spend on needs.
ww.To replace the need for income in life: A plan cannot replace income, because income pays for everything; the plan helps you manage and use the income you receive effectively.
ww.To increase the taxes a person pays: A good plan aims to manage money and often to reduce taxes legally, so increasing the taxes a person pays is not its purpose.

rw: Starting a family adds dependents and costs, so life insurance, health coverage and savings for children become much more important than before.

ww.Buying new shoes: Buying new shoes is a small purchase that does not change financial responsibilities, so it does not meaningfully increase the need for insurance or savings.
ww.Getting a free coupon: Getting a free coupon is a minor event with no lasting effect on financial responsibilities, so it does not raise insurance or savings needs.
ww.Picking a TV show: Picking a TV show is entertainment and changes no financial obligations, so it does not raise the need for insurance or savings.

rw: A bank takes deposits from savers and lends that money to borrowers, earning a profit from the difference in interest rates on each side.

ww.A government office that prints the mone: Governments, through treasuries and mints, print money; a bank is a private institution that holds deposits and makes loans, and does not print currency.
ww.A company that only sells insurance plan: A company that only sells insurance plans is an insurer; a bank takes deposits, pays interest, makes loans and provides payment services as its core business.
ww.A store that sells only gold and jewelry: A store selling only gold and jewelry is a retailer; banks are financial institutions that deal in deposits, loans and payments rather than in goods.

rw: Credit unions are owned by their members and run not for profit, while commercial banks are owned by shareholders who expect profit from the bank.

ww.Credit unions cannot offer savings accou: Credit unions do offer savings accounts to members, often called share accounts; saying they cannot is false, as these accounts are a core product.
ww.Credit unions are owned by the federal g: Credit unions are cooperatives owned by their members, not by the federal government; the government only supervises them through the NCUA.
ww.Commercial banks cannot make loans to an: Commercial banks make loans to many borrowers, including mortgages, car loans and business loans, as lending is a core part of their business.

rw: The NCUA insures credit union deposits, up to $250,000 per member, through its National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund, similar to FDIC coverage for banks.

ww.The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) in th: The IRS collects taxes and enforces tax law, so it does not insure deposits at credit unions; deposit insurance there comes from the NCUA.
ww.The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) in th: The FTC protects consumers from unfair business practices and deceptive advertising but does not insure deposits; credit union deposits are insured by the NCUA.
ww.The Securities and Exchange Commission i: The SEC regulates securities markets and investor protection; it does not insure deposits, which at credit unions are covered by the NCUA.

rw: Checking accounts are built for daily spending, bill payments, debit card use and writing checks, with quick access to cash at any time.

ww.Earning the highest stock returns: High stock returns come from investing in a brokerage account; a checking account earns little interest and is not designed for investment growth.
ww.Locking away money for twenty years: Locking money away for twenty years suits retirement accounts, not checking, which is made for access to funds that are used regularly.
ww.Borrowing money to buy a new home: Borrowing for a home is done through a mortgage loan; a checking account holds your own deposited money and does not lend to you.

rw: A savings account holds money you are not spending right away and pays interest on the balance, making it suited to goals and emergencies.

ww.Paying all your bills with paper checks: Paying bills with paper checks daily is what a checking account is for; savings accounts are intended for setting money aside, not frequent payments.
ww.Buying shares in companies directly onli: Buying shares directly happens in a brokerage account; a savings account holds deposits that earn interest and is not used to purchase securities.
ww.Taking out loans for large purchases onl: Taking out loans is done with lenders through loan accounts; a savings account holds your own deposits and does not provide borrowed money.

rw: A CD holds a deposit for a fixed term, such as 12 months, at a fixed rate, and early withdrawal usually triggers a penalty.

ww.A savings account with unlimited free wi: A savings account with unlimited free withdrawals at any time describes a flexible account; CDs lock funds until maturity, with penalties for early withdrawal.
ww.A stock that pays dividends every quarte: A stock paying quarterly dividends is an equity investment; a CD is a bank deposit with a fixed term and rate, not shares of a company.
ww.A loan that must be repaid in full withi: A loan repaid in one day is a very short loan; a CD is a deposit product where you lend money to the bank for a fixed term.

rw: A money market account is a deposit account that usually pays more than regular savings but limits the number of monthly transactions and may require a higher balance.

ww.A retirement account with tax penalties: A retirement account with penalties on any use describes an IRA or 401(k); a money market account is a deposit account that is not tied to retirement.
ww.A stock market account for buying public: A stock market account for buying shares is a brokerage account; a money market account is a bank deposit account that is safe and insured, not high risk.
ww.A loan account for buying a car or a tru: A car loan is borrowing from a lender; a money market account is a deposit account where you hold your own savings.

rw: Without costs for branches and tellers, online banks can pay higher interest on savings and charge lower fees, passing their savings to customers.

ww.Customers can deposit cash at a local br: Local branch deposits are a feature of traditional banks; an online-only bank has no physical branches, so cash deposits at a branch are not available.
ww.Customers get free vacations and gifts f: Online banks do not give free vacations as a rule; their benefits are financial, mainly lower fees and better rates, not gifts or prizes.
ww.Deposits are never insured by any progra: Reputable online-only banks are FDIC insured up to $250,000 per depositor, so claiming deposits are never insured is false and unhelpful.

rw: Overdraft protection pays a transaction when the account balance is too low, typically by drawing from a linked savings account or credit line, avoiding declines.

ww.A service that shields accounts from all: Overdraft protection has nothing to do with taxes; it covers payments when your account lacks funds, by linking a backup source or a credit line.
ww.A service that stops all purchases forev: It does not block every purchase; it helps transactions go through when funds are short, so a service that stops valid purchases is the opposite.
ww.A service that raises the interest rate: Overdraft protection does not change interest paid on the balance; it covers shortfalls when a payment is larger than the available funds in the account.

rw: An ATM, short for automated teller machine, lets customers withdraw cash, deposit money and check balances at any hour without needing to visit a teller.

ww.An account that matches your savings: An account that matches your savings is an employer match or a savings feature; an ATM is a machine that handles cash deposits and withdrawals.
ww.An annual tax measure for municipalities: An annual tax measure for municipalities has nothing to do with ATMs; these are cash machines run by banks and other financial service providers.
ww.An approved trading method for stocks: An approved trading method for stocks is not what ATM means; the machine handles cash and account transactions, not securities trading in the market.

rw: A debit card pulls money directly from your checking account when you pay, so the purchase is covered by funds you already hold.

ww.A card that earns interest on your depos: Earning interest on deposits describes a savings account, not a debit card; a debit card is a payment tool that draws on money already in your account.
ww.A card that lets you borrow from a lende: Borrowing from a lender and repaying with interest describes a credit card; a debit card spends your own money, so there is no loan or interest.
ww.A card that is used only for ATM balance: Debit cards work for purchases and ATM withdrawals as well as balance checks, so limiting them to balance checks at a branch is wrong.

rw: A credit card lends you money up to a set limit for purchases, which you repay later, and unpaid balances accrue interest.

ww.A card that gives you free money each mo: A credit card does not give free money; it is a loan that must be repaid, and unpaid balances accrue interest charges over time.
ww.A card that works only at your own bank': Credit cards work at millions of merchants and at ATMs worldwide, not only at one bank's machines, so limiting them to one bank's ATMs is wrong.
ww.A card that takes money straight from yo: Taking money straight from your checking account describes a debit card; a credit card instead borrows from the issuer, to be repaid later.

rw: You load a prepaid card with money in advance and can spend only that amount, so it works until the loaded balance runs out.

ww.A card that works only for online bankin: Prepaid cards can be used in stores and online as well as for banking; they are not limited to online banking, so that claim is wrong.
ww.A card that bills you after you spend: A card that bills you after you spend describes a credit or charge card; a prepaid card requires money to be loaded before you spend.
ww.A card that has an unlimited balance for: Prepaid cards are limited to the amount loaded; an unlimited balance would require credit, so claiming unlimited use does not describe them.

rw: APY stands for Annual Percentage Yield, the real rate of return earned in a year on a deposit after compounding is taken into account.

ww.Annual Payment Year: Annual Payment Year is not a real banking term; APY stands for annual percentage yield, a measure of the interest earned over a year including compounding.
ww.Accrued Principal Yield: Accrued Principal Yield is not the meaning; APY stands for annual percentage yield, which accounts for how often interest compounds during the year.
ww.Average Percent Yearly: Average Percent Yearly is not what the letters mean; APY stands for annual percentage yield, a standard way to compare savings accounts and their returns.

rw: Daily compounding adds interest to the balance more often, so later interest is earned on earlier interest; A's APY is about 4.08 percent compared with B's 4.00 percent.

ww.Neither earns anything on the money in i: Both accounts earn interest at a 4 percent rate, so neither is zero; saying nothing is earned ignores that savings accounts pay interest on balances.
ww.Account B, because annual compounding gi: Annual compounding adds interest only once a year, which gives a smaller result than daily compounding at the same rate, so B does not earn more.
ww.They earn exactly the same amount of int: The amounts are not equal, because compounding frequency matters; daily compounding earns slightly more than annual at the same 4 percent rate, as interest builds on interest.

rw: A payday loan is a small, short-term loan with high fees that is due on your next payday, which is why it is considered costly.

ww.A loan with no fees and no interest at a: Payday loans charge high fees and interest, often equal to triple digit annual rates, so a loan with no fees and no interest does not describe them.
ww.A long-term low-cost loan from a credit: A long-term low-cost loan from a credit union describes a different product; payday loans are short and expensive, usually repaid within weeks.
ww.A government grant that never needs repa: A government grant need not be repaid, but a payday loan must be repaid, typically in full plus fees on the next payday.

rw: High fees and short due dates make it hard to repay in full, so borrowers renew or take new loans, falling into a repeating debt trap.

ww.They are repaid over thirty years in equ: Payday loans are repaid in weeks, usually on the next payday, not over thirty years in equal parts, which describes a mortgage instead.
ww.They are insured by the government again: Payday loans are not government insured against loss; lenders carry the risk and charge high fees, and borrowers bear the burden if they cannot repay.
ww.They offer the lowest interest rates on: Payday loans have some of the highest costs, with fees equal to annual rates of several hundred percent, so offering the lowest rates is false.

rw: A mortgage lender provides a loan to buy real estate, with the property serving as collateral, so the lender can foreclose if payments stop.

ww.A deposit account for monthly bills and: A deposit account for bills and savings is offered by a bank or credit union; a mortgage lender's product is a home loan, not a deposit account.
ww.An insurance policy for a car or a truck: A car insurance policy comes from an insurer; a mortgage lender provides a loan for real estate and does not provide insurance coverage for vehicles.
ww.A loan used to buy stocks without any co: A mortgage is secured by the property, so it is not an unsecured loan, and mortgage money is used for real estate rather than for buying stocks.

rw: A stockbroker executes orders to buy and sell securities such as stocks and bonds on behalf of clients, usually earning a commission or fee.

ww.Prepares tax returns for individuals eac: Preparing tax returns is the work of an accountant or tax preparer; a stockbroker handles securities transactions for clients, not their tax filings or returns.
ww.Issues credit cards to consumers and sma: Issuing credit cards is done by banks and card issuers; a stockbroker buys and sells securities for clients and does not issue credit to customers.
ww.Insures homes against fire damage and ot: Insuring homes against fire is the job of an insurance company; a stockbroker works in investments and securities, not in property or casualty coverage.

rw: A financial advisor guides clients on saving, investing and planning for goals such as retirement, education and insurance, based on their personal circumstances.

ww.Collects debts for creditors and lenders: Collecting debts for creditors is the work of a collection agency; a financial advisor helps clients plan, save and invest, rather than pursue debtors.
ww.Prints currency for the federal state: Printing currency is done by government agencies like the Bureau of Engraving and Printing; a financial advisor gives money advice to individuals and families.
ww.Audits publicly traded companies yearly: Auditing public companies is done by accounting firms; a financial advisor works with individuals on money plans, not on company audits or annual reports.

rw: A fiduciary is legally bound to act in the client's best interest, which means placing the client's needs ahead of the advisor's own profit.

ww.They must maximize their own commissions: A fiduciary must put the client's interest first, not their own commissions, so maximizing their own commissions would directly breach the duty.
ww.They are paid only by the government age: Fiduciaries can be paid by clients through fees; being paid only by a government agency is not part of what the term means.
ww.They may sell any product without disclo: Fiduciaries must disclose conflicts and costs, so selling any product without disclosure would violate their duty; the term demands transparency and honesty.

rw: Insurance companies collect premiums from many people and use the pool to pay the claims of the few who suffer losses, spreading risk.

ww.Trading stocks for clients and firms: Trading stocks for clients is a brokerage function; an insurance company's main role is to take premiums and pay claims, not to buy securities for others.
ww.Lending money for home purchases to all: Lending money for home purchases is done by mortgage lenders and banks; insurers protect against loss, although some also invest, which is not their main role.
ww.Printing money for the national economy: Printing money is a government function carried out by mints and central banks; insurance companies manage risk and do not create currency for the economy.

rw: A pawnshop gives a loan against a personal item held as collateral, such as jewelry; if the borrower does not repay, the shop keeps the item.

ww.A bank that offers free checking account: A bank offers free checking accounts, deposits and many other services; a pawnshop is a different business that lends cash against items left as collateral.
ww.A store that sells new electronics only: Selling only new electronics describes a retailer; a pawnshop lends money against personal items and also resells items that owners fail to reclaim.
ww.A credit union branch office in the town: A credit union branch is a member-owned financial institution; a pawnshop is a for-profit business that lends against items and is not a credit union.

rw: A check cashing service cashes checks for a fee, giving people cash without needing a bank account, though the fees can be high compared with banks.

ww.A government agency that issues checks: Governments issue some checks, but a check cashing service is a private business that cashes checks for a fee, not an agency that issues them.
ww.A service that insures checks for a fee: Insuring checks is not what these businesses do; a check cashing service pays out cash for a check and charges a fee for the service.
ww.A bank service that gives free loans: Check cashing services charge fees and do not give free loans; a bank service giving free loans is not what such a business provides.

rw: A mobile payment app lets users send and receive money, pay merchants and split bills using a smartphone, without cash or a physical card.

ww.Printing paper statements at home for a: Printing paper statements is a bank back-office task; a mobile payment app is software on a phone that moves money electronically, not a printing tool.
ww.Setting the interest rate on a loan from: Interest rates on loans are set by lenders; a mobile payment app moves money between people and merchants and does not set rates on any loan.
ww.Filing taxes with the government each sp: Filing taxes is done with the tax authority using tax forms or software; a mobile payment app is meant for moving money, not for filing returns.

rw: P2P lending connects individual lenders with borrowers through an online platform, skipping the traditional bank, and lenders earn interest while taking on the risk of default.

ww.A bank lending only to other banks and b: Banks lending only to other banks describes interbank lending; peer-to-peer lending matches individual borrowers directly with individual or group lenders through an online platform.
ww.A store lending products to customers fo: A store lending products for a fee is rental or layaway; P2P lending involves individuals lending money directly to other individuals through an online service.
ww.The government lending money to citizens: Government lending is a different arrangement; peer-to-peer lending involves private people as lenders, matched with borrowers on an online platform, not state loans.

rw: A safe deposit box is a locked box in a bank vault where you store valuables and important documents such as deeds, passports and jewelry.

ww.A loan offered only to retirees who own: A loan for retirees who own homes outright describes a reverse mortgage; a safe deposit box is physical storage, not a loan of any kind.
ww.A savings account that cannot lose money: A savings account that cannot lose money is a deposit account; a safe deposit box is a storage container, not an interest-paying account.
ww.An online password manager used to keep: An online password manager is software that stores logins; a safe deposit box is a physical locked box kept inside a bank vault for valuables.
